# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–31 (Complete – Updated 2026-10-13)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: Autumn of eighth year after Waterloo (1830). Evening of Tuesday following Fisker's departure on Saturday, 19th April.
- **Key Locations**: London (Welbeck Street, Grosvenor Square, Abchurch Lane, Beargarden Club, Langham Hotel, Euston Square Railway Station, Bruton Street, Lincoln's Inn); Coventry Island; Queen's Crawley; Coldcombe and Mirecombe farms; Bryngate; Pumpernickel; Ostend; Hampshire ("the Evergreens"); Brussels; Aix-la-Chapelle; Bath and Cheltenham; Carbury Hall; Carbury Chase; Caversham; Sussex; Quenwick; various American locations.

## Major Deaths
- **John Sedley**: Died peacefully; buried at Brompton.
- **Mr. Osborne**: Deceased (four days after stroke); Major Dobbin appointed executor; Georgy established as heir.
- **Joseph Sedley**: Died at Aix-la-Chapelle three months after Dobbin's final visit. Heavily insured (£2,000); legacy split equally between Amelia and Rebecca (administratrix).
- **Colonel Rawdon Crawley**: Died of yellow fever at Coventry Island; estate devolved upon Sir Pitt's son, now Sir Rawdon Crawley, Bart.
- **Sir Pitt**: Died six weeks after Colonel Rawdon.

## Rebecca's Arc
**Seduction and Enslavement of Jos Sedley**: At Pumpernickel, Rebecca (Madame de Raudon, formerly with Rawdon Crawley) seduced Jos through calculated performance. Led him to Room No. 92, Elephant lodging-house. Jos became her "entirely slave." Lived in Brussels hotel in genteel manner. Jos died three months later at Aix-la-Chapelle. Insurance company challenged £2,000 payment; Rebecca prevailed. **Dobbin sent back his share and rigidly declined communication.**

**Final State**: Never became Lady Crawley though styles herself so. Son (Sir Rawdon, young baronet) declines to see her; receives liberal allowance. Appears very wealthy. Chiefly at Bath and Cheltenham; strong party considers her "most injured woman." Busies herself in piety, church attendance, Charity Lists.

## Amelia and William Dobbin
**Resolution**: At Ostend, Becky revealed George Osborne was "selfish humbug, low-bred cockney dandy" who wanted her to run away with him—"Dobbin forced him to keep his word." Emmy's internal struggle resolved: "There is nothing to forbid me now...I may love him with all my heart now."

**Marriage and Life**: Two mornings later at Dike, Amelia went to Dobbin "in dripping white bonnet and shawl...kissing one of his hands with all her might." Only Georgy and Jos present. Emmy told William: "Never speak of that day again." Dobbin quit service immediately, rented "the Evergreens" (Hampshire). Devoted father; fonder of daughter Jane (christened by Rev. James Crawley) than of his History of the Punjaub. Lady Jane godmother to daughter; they became great friends.

## Lady Carbury and Family

**Lady Carbury**: Lives modestly on Welbeck Street with son Felix and daughter Henrietta. "The woman was false from head to foot, but there was much of good in her, false though she was." Devoted to children, especially Felix. Back drawing-room serves as workspace for writing.

**Literary Work**: Authored "Criminal Queens"—work pandering to bad tastes through fabricated crime. **Crushed by "Evening Pulpit" review by Mr. Jones (Mr. Alf's reviewer), though errors lay near surface. Lady Carbury attempted proving error (man arrived Paris 1522, not earlier); visited publisher Mr. Leadham at Yarlton, received small cheque despite facts being irrelevant to judgment. Leadham advised never fighting newspapers. However, "Morning Breakfast Table" review by Mr. Broune (after receiving letter in first chapter) devoted two columns, praised work as delightful mixture, product of infinite research and brilliant imagination. Broune gave order "with good will."**

**Mr. Alf's Position (Chapter 31)**: **Mr. Alf states he never writes reviews himself; endeavours to get trustworthy judges. When judgment hostile to personal friend, he laments "accident" and trusts friend can "divide me as an individual from that Mr. Alf who has the misfortune to edit a newspaper." Lady Carbury disbelieves him entirely, thinking rightly that Mr. Jones took direct orders from Alf regarding "Criminal Queens" treatment. Yet she remembers intention to write another book and resolve to "conquer even Mr. Alf by spirit and courage under her present infliction."**

**Felix Carbury** (son): Beautiful as a star; cynosure of mother's eyes. Mother spoilt him; almost proud of his vices. Won £2,000 from Lord Grasslough and £400 from Miles Grendall at gaming (retained winnings). **Considering courtship of Marie Melmotte (great heiress); at Melmotte ball, waltzes with Marie, studying words ("I do") to convince her he could love her.** Since Roger's offer to Henrietta, Felix "gone on from bad to worse, till his condition had become one of hopeless embarrassment."

**Financial Crisis and Resolution (Chapter 31)**: **Herr Vossner convened second conference with Lords (Nidderdale and Grasslough), Miles Grendall, Sir Felix, and Paul Montague. Miles undertook to pay Vossner £450 at three months' end, endorsed by both lords, Sir Felix, and Montague. In return, Vossner produced £322 10s. in notes and gold. Felix became Director of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company.** Lady Carbury elated by discovery, though knowing son "could not lend assistance by his work to any company or commercial enterprise." **At evening party (Tuesday after Fisker's departure), Lady Carbury observed Felix ask Marie Melmotte—watched whispering, cool effrontery, girl's timid face and nervous twitching. As woman who understood such things, disapproved his manner greatly; but "if it might be successful...how glorious should her son be to her."**

**Mother's Vigil (Chapter 31)**: **Lady Carbury sat up entire night waiting for Felix in dining-room with volume of French memoirs, hoping to hear tidings of fortune. Disembarrassed herself of finery, wrapped in white dressing-gown. Acknowledged age stealing on her—short grey hairs over ears and temples, wrinkles round eyes, weariness round mouth. Yet not unhappy because growing old; her happiness, like most, was "ever in the future,--never reached but always coming." Great fears and hopes centred on Felix. Would not care how grey her hair if he married heiress; nothing that pearl-powder or "Morning Breakfast Table" could do would avail unless he extricated from ruin surrounding him.**

**Henrietta Carbury** (daughter): Romance with cousin Roger Carbury (nearly forty) and Paul Montague. Roger offered hand passionately. Paul fell in love during second visit to Carbury Hall. Hot-worded scene between Roger and Paul lasted above an hour; Paul packed and departed in tears. Roger blessed him at platform. **Henrietta rejected Roger's suit, claiming too young and age disparity insurmountable; admitted "even that disparity was not now her strongest reason."** Within week, Paul returned "as a still dear friend," having promised not to see Henrietta for three months but nothing further. Paul doubts his finances but declared he has money and won't give up Henrietta. Roger will not accede to justice of Paul's argument and remains firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle.

**Whitsun Week Plans (Chapter 31)**: Lady Carbury proposed to visit Carbury Manor for Whitsun week (arriving 20th May, staying over Sunday), intending to bring Henrietta and Felix (Felix would visit shorter time). Roger invited Paul Montague simultaneously. Upon learning both parties would attend, Roger wrote to Paul apologizing for inconvenience, stating: "After what has passed between us I need hardly say that I could not make you both welcome here together." Paul accepted postponement, remaining in town. Roger prepared ladies' rooms with care, particularly the smaller white-hangings room (sweet with May flowers) for Henrietta, placing white rose from hot-house on dressing table, believing "Surely she would know who put it there."

## The Melmottes

**Augustus Melmotte**: Arrived London from Paris within two years; previously M. Melmotte. Claims English birth though speaks with accent betraying "long expatriation." In City, his name "worth any money." Big man with large whiskers, rough hair, expression of mental power on harsh vulgar face. Magnificent in expenditure, successful in business. **Miles Grendall serves as usher/secretary in office.** **Chairman of South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Company with two million dollars of shares allocated to himself. Taken up old Longestaffe's affairs, means to put them straight. Has Caversham property and old Sussex property; bother because Dolly won't join father in selling.**

**Madame Melmotte**: Said Bohemian Jewess; speaks very little English.

**Marie Melmotte**: Speaks English well as foreigner. **Has begun forming own opinions; absolutely rejected Lord Grasslough (bankrupt, no income, ugly, vicious, ill-tempered).** Had experience with Lord Nidderdale. **People saying if Sir Felix Carbury managed affairs well he might be the happy man.**

## South Central Pacific and Mexican Railway Scheme

**The Enterprise**: Railway from Salt Lake City, branching from San Francisco and Chicago line, passing through New Mexico and Arizona into Mexico, terminating at Vera Cruz. Distance approximately 2,000 miles. Fisker considers cost questions "beside the mark and childish." Concession obtained from United States Government; correspondence maintained with President of Mexican Republic.

**Financial Strategy**: Stock at par; shares sold at premium to "run them up even to 110," yielding three hundred thousand dollars minimum. Directors understood fortune made by floating shares, not making actual railway—all whispered convictions on this.

**Launch and Direction (Chapter 31)**: **At fortnight's end from Fisker's arrival, company fully launched with London directors: Melmotte (chairman), Lord Alfred Grendall, Sir Felix Carbury, Samuel Cohenlupe (Member of Parliament for Staines, Jewish persuasion), Lord Nidderdale, and Paul Montague.**

**Fisker's Departure (Chapter 31)**: **Fisker started Saturday morning, 19th April, leaving Sir Felix at Club about seven. At railway station, met by Nidderdale and Montague; Nidderdale noted English pay up "when we can," contrasting Fisker. Fisker satisfied with scheme launch.**

**Paul Montague**: Junior member of firm. English. Personally dislikes Fisker but unable to resist his combination. Trembles for his money. Met Fisker at Liverpool great railway hotel; Fisker displayed maps, schedules, programmes. **Letter from Langham Hotel, posted at Euston Square, invited Melmotte to meet. Paul and Fisker travelled to London together next morning. Paul taking to living at Beargarden; reasoned man dines cheaper. Saw good deal of Sir Felix, Lord Nidderdale; entertained Lord Alfred once; dined twice with Melmotte in Grosvenor Square. Fisker suggested Paul enter for "great Marie Melmotte plate." Greatness of operations relieved from small expenses; champagne consumption increased. Paul found he could not wake up on London mornings with satisfactory thoughts as at Carbury Hall.** **At Beargarden cardroom, offered to undertake Grendall's debt himself; disallowed—he had only lately come, had no dealing in I.O.U.'s, last man responsible for Grendall's impecuniosity.**

## Roger Carbury
Nearly forty years old. Never owed shilling he could not pay; father likewise. Carbury parish named for family. Carbury Chase unfortunately belongs entirely to Bundlesham estate. Remains firmly opposed to Melmotte connection on principle; holds old-fashioned idea that "touching of pitch will defile." Took degree at Oxford; became what called "pervert," supposed "convert." Works as priest earning approximately day-labourer's wages, forced to buy second-hand clothes. Described as "certainly...a gentleman."

## The Longestaffes

**Sir Merton Longestaffe**: Owns properties in Sussex and Caversham. **At present moment, great desire to sell smaller property (Pickering) and disembarrass other (Caversham from debt). Debt not altogether of his own making; arrangement would serve whole family. Dolly refused to consent to Pickering sale unless half produce given to him at once for his own mortgaged estate. Consequence: Pickering could not be sold. Mr. Longestaffe determined no more London expenses that year, announcing family will not return to London from Caversham. Struggled to maintain dignified tranquillity; voice quivered with emotion. Told family what must be done in town must be done this week.**

**Georgiana Longestaffe** (daughter): Supposed to have strongest head and sharpest tongue among Longestaffes. **Gave strong-minded protest against Melmottes; thinks horrible to have "these sort of people brought down upon us at Caversham. No one knows who they are, or where they came from, or what they'll turn to." Threatened to stay in London with Mrs. Primero (whom she dislikes and calls vulgar) rather than be "buried down in that place for a whole year." Called Madame Melmotte "not half so vulgar" as her vulgarity. **Protested Caversham costs more than London, is dullest house in England. Suggested father shut Caversham entirely and go abroad if economy desired. Family party evening in Bruton Street was gloomily silent; girls would not speak to father, answered monosyllables. Lady Pomona ill, wiping eyes, having learned of Dolly's refusal upstairs.**

**Adolphus (Dolly) Longestaffe** (son): Has rooms of own in Bruton Street; seldom dines with family. Mother writes notes without end pressing invitations; Dolly barely reads, never answers—opens, thrusts into pocket, forgets. Consequently mother worships him; sisters treat him with deference. Could do as he liked; sisters felt themselves slaves bound by dulness of Longestaffe regime. **Conversation with father in study regarding sale of property. Made woful grimace at sisters before following father out; sisters expected not to see him for month, knowing he and squire never came together without quarrelling. Obdurate regarding his own rights in dealings with father.**
